title: Zechariah 14:12–21
context: The prophet continues. The LORD will strike the peoples who fought against Jerusalem with a plague, described in stark terms that picture their strength wasting away, and a panic from the LORD will turn them against one another, as in earlier battles (compare Judges 7:22; 2 Chronicles 20:23). Judah will fight at Jerusalem, and the wealth of the nations will be gathered; a like plague will fall on the animals in the camps. Then the survivors of the nations will go up year by year to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, and to keep the feast of booths (compare Leviticus 23:34–43; Isaiah 2:2–3); families who do not go up will have no rain, and Egypt is named in particular. In that day HOLY TO THE LORD, the inscription once worn on the high priest’s turban (Exodus 28:36), will be on the bells of the horses, the common pots will be as holy as the altar bowls, and there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD. The word rendered Canaanite can also mean trader or merchant, and some readers connect the line with Jesus clearing the temple (compare John 2:16). Readers take chapter 14 in historic, symbolic, and future senses: some see the oracle fulfilled in events after the exile and in the coming of Christ, some read it as a symbolic picture of God’s victory and the gathering of the nations into his worship, and some expect a future fulfillment at the Lord’s return. Each of these readings appears among both Arminian and Reformed readers, and the question of the millennium does not divide the traditions as such. Shared ground: Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat the worship of the nations and the holiness of all of life as common hope.

verses.text: This will be the plague with which the LORD will strike all the peoples who have fought against Jerusalem: their flesh will consume away while they stand on their feet, and their eyes will consume away in their sockets, and their tongue will consume away in their mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD striking the peoples who fought against Jerusalem with a plague. Opposition to God ends in ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment on those who attack his people, described in stark poetic terms. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse soberly, without dwelling on its imagery.

verses.text: It will happen in that day that a great panic from the LORD will be among them; and they will each seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand will rise up against the hand of his neighbor.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a panic from the LORD turning the enemies against one another. God confounds those who oppose him and his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a pattern from earlier battles (compare Judges 7:22; 2 Chronicles 20:23). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as God defending his people.

verses.text: Judah also will fight at Jerusalem; and the wealth of all the surrounding nations will be gathered together: gold, silver, and clothing, in great abundance.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Judah fighting at Jerusalem and the wealth of the nations gathered. What was plundered is restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a reversal of 14:1, where Jerusalem’s plunder was divided. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as part of the vision’s picture of reversal.

verses.text: A plague like this will fall on the horse, on the mule, on the camel, on the donkey, and on all the animals that will be in those camps.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the plague falling also on the animals in the enemy camps. The judgment on the attackers is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the thoroughness of God’s judgment on the attacking armies. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse soberly, as part of the vision’s poetic language.

verses.text: It will happen that everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up from year to year to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, and to keep the feast of booths.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see survivors of the nations going up yearly to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, and keep the feast of booths. Former enemies become worshipers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the nations gathered into the worship of the LORD (compare Isaiah 2:2–3; Isaiah 66:23). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for the nations, held in more than one sense.

verses.text: It will be that whoever of all the families of the earth doesn’t go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, on them there will be no rain.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see that families who refuse to go up to worship will have no rain. Refusing to worship God brings real loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant consequences extended to the nations (compare Deuteronomy 11:17). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as showing that worship of the King is not optional.

verses.text: If the family of Egypt doesn’t go up and doesn’t come, neither will it rain on them. This will be the plague with which the LORD will strike the nations that don’t go up to keep the feast of booths.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Egypt named among those who will suffer if they refuse to go up. Even the great powers are accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Egypt, Israel’s ancient oppressor, called to worship (compare Isaiah 19:21). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse within the vision’s picture of the nations under God.

verses.text: This will be the punishment of Egypt and the punishment of all the nations that don’t go up to keep the feast of booths.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see punishment for Egypt and all nations that refuse to keep the feast of booths. Accountability is universal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary of the warning in the previous verses. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as affirming God’s rule over every nation.

verses.text: In that day there will be inscribed on the bells of the horses, “HOLY TO THE LORD”; and the pots in the LORD’s house will be like the bowls before the altar.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see HOLY TO THE LORD inscribed on the horses’ bells and the pots as holy as the altar bowls. Ordinary things become holy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the high priest’s inscription (Exodus 28:36) spread to common things. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a picture of all of life consecrated to God.

verses.text: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the LORD of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see every pot in Jerusalem and Judah holy to the LORD of Armies, and no Canaanite in his house. Holiness fills everyday life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s house free of anything unclean or profane, and some connect the line with John 2:16 (compare Revelation 21:27). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for a fully consecrated people.
